name: Deadlist — is this list still real?
one_liner: Paste any list — your SaaS subscriptions, a 'top 50 AI tools' blog post, your CRM accounts, your bookmarks — and Deadlist tells you which of them are dead, acquired, renamed or pivoted, each with a citation and a date.
problem: For anyone who keeps a list of companies or products — indie hackers with a 'tools I use' page, VCs with a tracking sheet, writers maintaining a roundup post, ops people with a vendor list, anyone with a folder of startup bookmarks. Lists rot silently: companies shut down, get acquired, rebrand, or quietly stop shipping, and nothing in the list changes colour. Checking 40 of them by hand is ~40 minutes of opening tabs, reading a homepage, squinting at a 'we've been acquired' banner, and guessing. Deadlist makes that one paste and twenty seconds, and the output is a scoreboard you want to screenshot: 'Of your 38 tools, 6 are dead, 4 were acquired, 2 renamed.'
target_customer: Indie hackers and builders on X, VC analysts and scouts, newsletter and roundup writers, r/SaaS and Hacker News readers, and ops people with vendor spreadsheets. They hang out on X, Hacker News, r/SaaS and r/indiehackers — all places where a 'your list is 23% dead' screenshot travels.
why_now: Parallel's Decisions API launched 27 Oct 2026: web-grounded typed answers (probability or category, with citations) at $0.001 per request for up to 100 batched questions, ~200ms-1s latency, 600 req/min, 5,000 free requests. That is the exact shape this needs — one batched call can status-check a whole 40-item list for a tenth of a cent, with evidence. Doing this six months ago meant a scraper, a search API bill and an LLM pass per row, which is why the free version does not exist.
comparables: Parallel's own launch page links demo examples including a YC company status checker and an archive tracker — closest prior art, but they are vendor demos of single narrow datasets, and the available sources do not show their code is open. Clay, Oppora and Clearbit-style enrichment do company data at scale but are paid, signup-gated, sales-focused, and answer firmographics rather than 'is this thing dead'. Autopsy.io and Startup Graveyard style sites are static curated lists of famous failures, not a checker for YOUR list. Link checkers (Check My Links, broken-link crawlers) test whether a URL 200s — a dead company's homepage often still 200s, and a thriving one can 404 a page. Deadlist differs by taking an arbitrary pasted list, resolving each item to an entity, and returning a *status verdict with a citation and a date*, free and open source with no signup.
risks: Could be a one-time toy — you check your list once, screenshot it, and never return; the counter is making re-checks cheap and giving a 'what changed since last time' diff, but that needs saved lists, which v1 deliberately cuts. Accuracy on obscure entities: a web-grounded model can confidently mark a quiet-but-alive two-person startup as dead, which is both unfair and embarrassing in public; mitigated by a prominent UNSURE bucket and always showing the citation. Hosted-demo cost and abuse: 5,000 free requests go fast if the post lands, so rate-limit per IP, cap list length, and ship bring-your-own-key from day one.
build_plan: Stack: single Next.js page on Vercel, TypeScript, one serverless route (the Parallel key must stay server-side — the API requires an x-api-key header and browser CORS is unconfirmed), Tailwind, no database, no auth. Steps: (1) Textarea that accepts a pasted list, a CSV, or a markdown bullet list; split to lines, cap at 60 items for the free demo. (2) Server route batches items into Decisions calls, asking per item: is this company/product still operating; was it acquired and by whom; did it change name; date of the most recent signal — typed outputs plus citations. (3) Render results as a colour-coded scoreboard: ALIVE / DEAD / ACQUIRED / RENAMED / UNSURE, each row showing the one-line reason, the date and a citation link; UNSURE is a first-class state and must never be dressed up as DEAD. (4) Headline stat at the top ('9 of your 38 are no longer what you think') plus a 'copy result card as image' button for sharing, and a 'download CSV' button. (5) Ship it open source on GitHub with the stack listed and a rate-limited hosted demo on the 5,000 free requests, with a 'bring your own API key' field so heavy users pay their own way. Cut: accounts, saved lists, scheduled re-checks, logos, any non-company entity types.
launch_post:
Paste a list of companies — your SaaS subscriptions, a 'top 50 AI tools' post, your bookmarks — and find out which ones are actually dead.

Deadlist checks each one against the live web and gives you ALIVE / DEAD / ACQUIRED / RENAMED with a citation.

My own stack: 6 of 38 were gone. Free + open source.
reasoning: Won the build track because it is the clearest one-input/one-surprising-output shape the taste file calls for — paste, wait, get a result you want to screenshot — and because its dependency is real, checked and dirt cheap ($0.001/request, 5,000 free, published rate limits). It beat the Genie 4 and LFM3 ideas on buildability: Genie 4 is waitlisted with no confirmed Gemini API access, and the LFM3 on-device ideas are a day of model plumbing before anything is visible. Different problem and audience from the venture: Deadlist is a free consumer-ish curiosity toy for builders and writers checking a pasted list, while Stalecheck is a paid recurring finance workflow inside an AP team's ledger. They share the observation that lists rot, not a workflow, a buyer or a product.
candidates_considered:
VENTURE
1. Stalecheck — continuous vendor-master refresh for mid-market AP teams (KEPT, lead). Real paid incumbents prove the pain, but all are quote-only and payment-time focused; the standing monthly file audit for a 400-supplier controller is unserved and newly cheap to deliver.
2. Grant/tender eligibility pre-screening for nonprofits and SMEs using web-grounded decisions (DROPPED). Instrumentl at $299-999/mo already does profile matching and owns the buyer; the "true eligibility check" sliver is legally fragile — a wrong pass/fail is worse than no answer — and the buyer is budget-poor.
3. Supplier/counterparty adverse-news monitoring for procurement (DROPPED). Owlin, RapidRatings, Coupa and Creditsafe already serve this buyer with this workflow at enterprise scale; no narrow unserved slice surfaced in search, and it is the same "monitor an entity" shape as the lead without the ledger wedge.
4. Cloud-exit / AWS-to-bare-metal migration as a productised service, from the Hetzner bookmark (DROPPED). A real market exists but it is already competed as consultancy (WZ-IT from €1,990, CloudExit Pro on 20% of savings) and it is a services business, not an agent-edge software venture — poor fit for this builder's profile.
5. Anything derived from skill-diet, Action Gateway or RWE-Bench (DROPPED AS REPEATS). Collide with SkillProof/SkillPeek, Doublecheck/Ledger/Driftwatch, and EvalSeed/AgentGauntlet respectively — same buyers, same core workflows.

BUILD
1. Deadlist — paste any list of companies, get ALIVE/DEAD/ACQUIRED/RENAMED with citations (KEPT, runner-up slot). Perfect one-input/one-output shape, every dependency price-checked, and the closest prior art is a vendor's own closed demo.
2. Genie 4 world-model toy, e.g. turn a photo into a walkable world (DROPPED). Most striking bookmark of the night by engagement, but access is waitlisted via Project Genie for Google AI Ultra subscribers with Gemini API availability unconfirmed — cannot ship this weekend.
3. On-device LFM3-Audio or LFM3-VL browser toy, e.g. a private local meeting-notes or video-describer (DROPPED). Weights are genuinely available on Hugging Face under the LFM Open License, but a day disappears into quantisation and runtime plumbing before anything is visible on screen, and the wow is "it runs locally" rather than the output itself.
4. Skill token-bloat visualiser from the skill-diet post (DROPPED). Repeat of SkillPeek's audience and workflow, and skill-diet itself plus several community skills already do the optimisation.
5. CSV row-enrichment playground ("ask a question about every row") (DROPPED). Directly the crowded Clay/Oppora/GPT-for-Sheets space with good free options already; Deadlist is the same technology aimed at one sharper, more shareable question.
research_notes:
Reading pot (3/3 used): summarised the Parallel Decisions API launch (confirmed $0.001/request for up to 100 batched questions, 5,000 free, 200ms-1s latency, citations, and what Jev/decision models are), RWE-Bench (20 tasks, 11 models, deterministic engineering verifiers — interesting but eval territory already in the library), and the LFM3 family (open weights on Hugging Face under the LFM Open License, GGUF/ONNX/MLX builds, d1-2B typed decisions self-hostable). I cannot see images or video, so the Genie 4, Cursor Annotate, Wonder and macOS-dock posts were judged on text plus search only.

Venture pot (11/12 used): checked DigitalOcean Action Gateway in detail (policy allow/ask/deny, $0.10 per 1,000 invocations) and used it to rule the whole agent-governance direction out as a library repeat. Then worked the back-office angle: searched insurance-broker AI (found Covera in YC, buyer already being served), procurement/supplier monitoring (Owlin, RapidRatings — enterprise, served), CRM data decay (Clay/ZoomInfo — wrong buyer, sales not finance), then narrowed to AP and vendor master. Summaries on Trustpair/nsKnox/Creditsafe and on Eftsure/Trustpair/nsKnox self-serve pricing produced the decisive finding: no published self-serve tier anywhere, nsKnox's own SMB page at $8,000/yr for 100 validations/month, Eftsure pricing scaled to annual expenditure. A further summary on Tipalti/Coupa/Basware/Apex established that continuous monitoring exists mainly inside full procurement suites with unpublished buyer pricing, and that scheduled audits of the *existing* NetSuite/Xero file are the unverified gap. Statistics summary surfaced CDQ-attributed ~21% annual record decay and ~16% duplicates plus an Infosys BPM sample at ~25% inactive/redundant — all labelled as directional, not industry benchmarks. A grant-eligibility summary and a UK Companies House monitoring search killed two alternative candidates (Instrumentl owns the grant buyer; FilingPing/Company Watch already do free registry alerts but never touch your ledger). This research is what moved the venture from a generic "web-grounded monitoring" idea to the specific CSV-in/worklist-out wedge priced under the incumbents.

Build pot (7/7 used): confirmed Genie 4 shipped 27 Oct 2026 but is waitlisted via Project Genie for AI Ultra subscribers with Gemini API access unconfirmed — that killed the highest-engagement build candidate. Searched skill token-optimisation tooling and found community skills already doing it, confirming the repeat. Searched fact-checking apps, one-click company due-diligence tools, CSV enrichment tools and "still in business" checkers: enrichment is crowded and paid, but no free, open, paste-a-list status checker surfaced. A final summary confirmed the Decisions API needs a server-side key, has a 600 req/min limit and a 5,000-request free tier, and that Parallel's own demos (including a YC company status checker) exist but are not verifiably open source — which set Deadlist's differentiation (arbitrary pasted lists, open source, explicit UNSURE state) and forced the serverless-route architecture into the build plan.
prototype_summary: Deadlist is a one-screen prototype where pasting a list of 20 company names streams in staggered, skeleton-loading verdict rows (alive/dead/acquired/renamed/unsure) with reasons and citations, a counting-up "7 of 20 are not what you think" stat card, filter chips, and a shareable result card modal.
